name: The Reckoning Table
goal: Evaluate an expression by hand and predict its type and value before running it.

description.what: How Python works an expression out: which operator acts first, what value comes back, and what type that value has.
description.why: A program is mostly expressions, and an expression that runs without complaining can still be quietly wrong - the wrong division, the wrong order, a number where a piece of text was needed.
description.enables: You will be able to look at a line of arithmetic, say what it produces and what type it produces, and be right before you press Run.
description.assumes: You can store a value under a name, print it, and ask what type a value has.
description.assessed: You will predict the output of expressions you have not run, complete and repair small pieces of arithmetic, and write code whose correctness depends on choosing the right operator.

lesson.title: Working It Out Before It Is Run

sections.title: An expression is something that becomes a value
sections.body:
An **expression** is any piece of Python that Python can work out into a single value. `7` is an expression - it is already a value. So is `7 + 2`, which becomes `9`. So is `price * 3`, which becomes whatever the name `price` is holding, multiplied by three. Working an expression out is called **evaluating** it, and what you are left with afterwards is one value and nothing else.

The symbols that do the working out are **operators**, and the values they act on are **operands**. Python gives you seven of them for numbers: `+` add, `-` subtract, `*` multiply, `/` divide, `//` divide and round down, `%` the remainder after dividing, and `**` raise to a power. Note that `*` is a star rather than the times sign of school arithmetic, and that `^` is not a power in Python - it means something else entirely, so using it gives you a wrong answer rather than an error.

Every value has a type, so every expression has a type as well as a value. `7 + 2` is an `int` with the value `9`. Predicting both is the habit this floor exists to build, because a program holding the right number of the wrong type breaks later, somewhere else, in a way that is much harder to trace back to the line that caused it.
sections.code:
print(7 + 2)
print(7 - 2)
print(7 * 2)
print(7 ** 2)
print(7 % 2)
print(type(7 + 2))

annotations.text: `**` is a power: 7 to the power of 2, which is 49. Two stars, not one - a single star here would give you 14.
`%` is the remainder: 2 goes into 7 three times with 1 left over, so this is 1. It is not a percent sign, whatever the shape of it suggests.
The expression is evaluated first, down to the single value 9, and only then is its type asked for. `type` never sees the `+` at all.

checkpoint.explain: `2 ** 5` is two multiplied by itself five times, which is 32 - reading it as 2 times 5 gives 10 and is the commonest slip. `17 % 5` is the remainder: 5 goes into 17 three times with 2 left over, so the answer is the leftover 2, not the three lots that fitted.

sections.title: Which operator goes first
sections.body:
`2 + 3 * 4` is `14`, not `20`. Python does not simply read left to right: each operator has a **precedence**, a rank that decides which one acts first, and multiplication outranks addition. So `3 * 4` is worked out first and the `2` is added to what it produced.

From strongest to weakest, the ranks you have so far are: anything inside brackets, then `**`, then a minus sign written in front of a single value, then `*` `/` `//` `%` sharing one rank, then `+` and `-` sharing a weaker one. Operators of the same rank are worked out left to right, so `10 - 4 - 3` means `(10 - 4) - 3`, which is `3` rather than `9`. The one exception is `**`, which groups right to left: `2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** 9`, or `512`.

Brackets beat every rank and cost nothing at all. When you know the order, brackets say so to the next reader; when you do not know it, brackets save you from guessing. `(2 + 3) * 4` cannot be misread by anybody, and neither can `2 + (3 * 4)`.

The trap worth memorising is `-2 ** 2`. The power binds tighter than the minus sign, so this is minus the value of two squared, which is `-4`. If you meant the square of minus two you have to write `(-2) ** 2`, and then you get `4`.

annotations.text: The brackets are worked out first, so this is 5 * 4 = 20. Same symbols as the line above, different answer - the order is not a detail.
`**` groups right to left, so this is 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512. Left to right would have given 8 ** 2 = 64.
The power acts before the minus, so this is -(2 ** 2) = -4. Write (-2) ** 2 if you meant to square a negative number.

checkpoint.explain: Three ranks in one line: the power first giving 9, then the multiplication giving 18, then the addition giving 19. Reading strictly left to right gives 81, which is what a calculator without precedence would tell you and what Python will never do.

sections.title: Two divisions, and turning one type into another
sections.body:
Python has two divisions and they answer different questions. `/` is **true division** and always hands back a `float`, even when the answer is exact: `6 / 3` is `2.0`, not `2`. `//` is **floor division**, which divides and then rounds down to a whole number, so `7 // 2` is `3`. Its partner `%` gives what was left over, so `7 % 2` is `1`. Together the pair answers "how many whole lots, and how much remains".

Rounding **down** is not the same as chopping the decimal part off, and negative numbers are where the difference shows: `-7 // 2` is `-4`, because -4 is below -3.5. If you want the chopping behaviour instead, `int(-3.5)` gives `-3`, because `int` always moves towards zero. Two reasonable-sounding rules, two different answers, and mixing them up produces results that are wrong by exactly one - the hardest size of error to notice.

`int()`, `float()` and `str()` are **conversions**: each takes a value and produces a new value of that type. The original is untouched, because they hand back a new value rather than changing the old one. `int("12")` is the number `12`, and `str(12)` is the two-character piece of text `"12"`.

You need conversion because Python refuses to guess. `"3" + 4` is a `TypeError` and stops the program, since `+` between text and a number could mean adding or joining and Python will not pick for you. But `"ab" * 3` is perfectly legal and gives `"ababab"` - repeating text a whole number of times has only one sensible meaning. So `"3" * 2` is `"33"`, not `6`, and that is not an error at all, which makes it far more dangerous than the one that crashes.
sections.code:
print(6 / 3)
print(7 // 2, -7 // 2)
print(7 % 2)
print(int(-3.7), int("12") + 1)
print("3" * 2)
print("total: " + str(12))

annotations.text: Exact, and still a float: 2.0. `/` never gives you an int, which is why a count of things should be built with `//`.
Rounding down, not chopping: -3.5 rounds down to -4. `int(-7 / 2)` would have given -3 instead.
`int("12")` is the number twelve, so adding 1 gives 13. Without that conversion the line would be a TypeError.
`str(12)` makes the text "12", which `+` can join to other text. This is how a number gets into a printed message.

checkpoint.explain: The first is a float even though the division came out exactly - writing `3` there is the natural guess and the wrong one. The other two split 9 into two whole fours with 1 left over, which is the pair of answers `//` and `%` always give you together.

sections.title: Shorthand, and the difference one symbol makes
sections.body:
`count = count + 1` reads the value under `count`, adds one, and stores the result back under the same name. It is so common that Python has a shorthand for it: `count += 1` means exactly that and nothing more. Every arithmetic operator has one - `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `//=`, `%=`, `**=` - and each is called an **augmented assignment**.

The shorthand keeps the type rules of the operator underneath it. `count /= 4` uses true division, so `count` becomes a float even if it was a whole number and the division came out exactly. If you wanted it to stay a whole number you needed `//=`.

Now the confusion that catches everybody, and it is worth naming out loud. A single `=` **stores**: it puts the value on the right under the name on the left, and asks nothing. A doubled `==` **compares**: it works out whether two values are equal and becomes `True` or `False`. `x = 3` changes `x`; `x == 3` leaves everything alone and merely answers a question. Writing one where you meant the other either destroys a value you needed or asks a question you never wanted asked.

So the habit this floor is really about: before you run anything, say what the value will be **and** what type it will be. Then run it. When you are right you have lost nothing; when you are wrong you have found a gap in exactly the place it would otherwise have cost you an hour. One note for the practice ahead - some tasks are shaped as a named box of work, a line beginning `def` and then a line beginning `return`, where the expression after `return` becomes the box's answer. Building those boxes is a later floor; here you only fill in the expression.
sections.code:
count = 10
count += 5
count *= 2
print(count)

count /= 4
print(count, type(count))

print(count == 7.5, count == "7.5")

annotations.text: Identical to `count = count + 5`. The right-hand side is worked out with the old value, then stored back under the same name.
`/=` is true division, so count is now the float 7.5 - the shorthand does not protect the type.
`==` compares and produces True or False. 7.5 and the text "7.5" are different types with different values, so the second answer is False.

checkpoint.explain: `+=` changed x to 10, then `==` merely asked whether it was 10 and answered True without changing anything. Had the last line used a single `=` it would have overwritten x rather than asking about it, which is the whole distinction sitting in one line.

guided-practice.prompt: Work each expression out by precedence before you answer. What does this print?
guided-practice.hint: Brackets first, then `**`, then `*`, then `+`. The three expressions use the same digits and give three different answers.
guided-practice.explain: The middle one is the only one that gives 20, and it gets there because brackets outrank everything else. Reading the first expression left to right also gives 20, which is exactly why that answer feels right and is wrong - the multiplication happens before the addition regardless of which was written first.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete this so it prints `5`. Use augmented assignment for both steps: add 5 to the score, then divide it down to a whole number by 3.
guided-practice.hint: Each blank is an operator with `=` stuck on the end. The second one has to leave the value a whole number.
guided-practice.explain: 15 divided by 3 is exactly 5, so `/=` would also reach the right number - but it would print `5.0`, because true division produces a float even when nothing is left over. The prompt asked for `5`, and only `//=` gives you that.

guided-practice.prompt:
Track the value stored under `total` after each line runs.

`total = 4`
`total *= 3`
`total -= 2`
`total //= 4`
`total /= 2`
guided-practice.hint: Each line works on the value the line before it left behind. Watch the type on the last two lines, not only the number.
guided-practice.explain: The third step drops 10 down to 2 because floor division rounds 2.5 down, and the last step turns a whole number into `1.0` because `/=` is true division. Writing `1` for that last answer is the natural response and misses the type change - which is precisely the change that would break a later line expecting a whole number.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `whole_minutes(seconds)` giving how many complete minutes fit into that many seconds. A partial minute does not count, so 130 seconds is 2 complete minutes. Use floor division so the answer is a whole number.
guided-practice.hint: One expression after `return`: divide by 60 with the operator that rounds down.
guided-practice.explain: The 59 case is the one that matters: true division would give 0.9833..., which is neither zero complete minutes nor anything a later line counting minutes could use. Floor division answers the question actually asked - how many whole lots fit - and the 120 case confirms it does not lose the exact one.

guided-practice.prompt: `label_total(count)` should hand back a message like `total: 5`. It stops with a `TypeError` on every call. Fix it, keeping the name `label_total`.
guided-practice.hint: `+` will not join text to a number. Convert the number to text first with `str()`.
guided-practice.explain: Python refuses `"total: " + 5` because `+` between text and a number has two plausible meanings and it will not choose one for you. The tempting fix is to swap the `+` for a comma, which works inside `print` but not here, because this has to produce a single piece of text rather than display two things side by side.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `stack_bonus(base)` which takes the starting score, adds 12 to it, doubles what that gives, then takes away 5, and hands back the result. So `stack_bonus(0)` is 19. Build it with augmented assignment, one step per line.
guided-practice.solution:
def stack_bonus(base):
    score = base
    score += 12
    score *= 2
    score -= 5
    return score
guided-practice.hint: Three lines between the two you were given, each of the shape `score ?= n`, in the order the prompt describes.
guided-practice.explain: Written as one expression this is `(base + 12) * 2 - 5`, and those brackets are compulsory - `base + 12 * 2 - 5` would multiply before adding and give a different answer for every input. Splitting it across augmented assignments removes the question entirely, because each line is one whole step, which is often the clearer way to write a calculation you had to stop and think about.

independent-practice.prompt: A shop advertises a percentage off. Write `sale_price(price, percent_off)` giving the amount actually payable, so `sale_price(200, 25)` is 150.
independent-practice.solution:
def sale_price(price, percent_off):
    return price - price * percent_off / 100
independent-practice.explain: The subtraction has to happen last, and it does so without any brackets because `*` and `/` both outrank `-` - but `(price - price * percent_off) / 100` is the same symbols grouped differently and gives a wildly different answer. The 7-at-half-off case shows why the result is a float: half of seven is not a whole number, and a price that could not be represented would be a real defect.

independent-practice.prompt: A photo album holds a fixed number of photos on each page, and a page that is only partly filled is still a page that had to be used. Write `pages_needed(photos, per_page)` giving how many pages are needed to hold them all. Ten photos at three to a page need 4 pages.
independent-practice.solution:
def pages_needed(photos, per_page):
    return (photos + per_page - 1) // per_page
independent-practice.explain: Rounding down is the opposite of what this problem wants, so the standard answer pushes the total up by one page-worth minus one before dividing, which tips any leftover over the line without disturbing an exact fit. The 9-and-3 test fails if you simply add a page unconditionally, and the 0 test fails if you add a page whenever there is a remainder without checking there is one.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `seconds_label(seconds)` giving a piece of text describing that duration in minutes and seconds, in the form `2m 10s` for 130 seconds. A duration under a minute still shows its zero, so 59 seconds is `0m 59s`.
independent-practice.explain: Two things have to be right at once: splitting 130 into whole lots and leftover, and getting numbers into a piece of text at all, which Python will not do on its own. The 120 case is the trap - its leftover is 0 and must still appear, so anything that drops a zero produces `2m s` and fails.

independent-practice.prompt: `is_balanced(paid, owed)` should report whether the amount paid matches the amount owed. It reports `True` every single time, including when it should not. Fix it, keeping the name `is_balanced`.
independent-practice.solution:
def is_balanced(paid, owed):
    return paid == owed
independent-practice.explain: The second line stores rather than asks: it throws away what was paid and replaces it with what was owed, so by the time the comparison runs the two are guaranteed to match. Nothing crashes and no warning appears, which is what makes a stray single `=` worse than a mistake Python rejects outright - the program keeps going and tells you what you hoped to hear.

choices: Divides and rounds the result down to a whole number
Divides and always gives a float
Marks the rest of the line as a comment
Gives the remainder left over after dividing
exam.explain: Rounding down is the definition; it is `/` that always gives a float and `%` that gives the leftover. The comment answer is worth knowing about, because `//` really does begin a comment in several other languages, which is why it looks wrong to anybody arriving from one of them.

exam.prompt: What is the difference between `=` and `==` in Python?
choices: `=` stores a value under a name; `==` works out whether two values are equal
They mean the same thing, and `==` is just the clearer spelling
`=` works out whether two values are equal; `==` stores a value under a name
exam.explain: One changes the world and one asks a question about it, and no amount of context makes them interchangeable. The last choice is the same distinction written backwards, and that is exactly the mix-up that leaves a name quietly overwritten by the value it was supposed to be checked against.

The power outranks both the division and the minus sign, so the first is 100 // 9 and the second is -(3 ** 2). Working the first left to right gives 1111 and reading the second as the square of minus three gives 9, and both wrong answers come from the same assumption that Python reads in writing order.

exam.code:
a = 7 / 2
b = 7 // 2
print(a, b, a == b)
exam.explain: The two divisions genuinely disagree here because 7 does not split evenly, so the comparison is False - and this is the case where the difference is obvious. It is when a division comes out exactly, and `4 / 2 == 4 // 2` is True while the types still differ, that the distinction gets quietly lost.

Multiplying text by a whole number repeats it, so two copies of the character 3 sit side by side and print as `33`. The expected answer is 6, and this is worth drilling because no error is raised: the program carries on holding the wrong value, unlike `"3" + 2`, which stops the moment it runs.

exam.prompt: Python is evaluating `2 + 12 // 2 ** 2`. Put the three steps into the order they actually happen.
exam.explain: The power is the strongest rank so it resolves first, then the floor division, and the addition last because `+` is the weakest of the three. Starting from the leftmost `+` is the natural reading and would give 14 // 4, which is 3 - a plausible-looking answer reached in entirely the wrong order.

exam.prompt:
Track the value stored under `n` after each line runs.

`n = 20`
`n //= 6`
`n **= 2`
`n %= 4`
`n -= 1`
exam.explain: Each line replaces `n` with the result of its operator applied to whatever `n` held, so an error at the first step follows you all the way to the end. The first step is where it usually goes wrong: 6 goes into 20 three times with 2 left over, and floor division keeps the 3 and discards the leftover entirely.

exam.prompt: `"3" + 4` stops the program with a TypeError, but `"3" * 4` runs happily and gives `"3333"`. Explain why Python treats these two differently, and say which of the two is more likely to cost you an afternoon.
exam.explain: `+` between text and a number has two plausible meanings - add the values, or join them into one piece of text - and Python refuses to guess, so it raises an error rather than picking. `*` by a whole number has only one sensible meaning, repeat the text that many times, so there is nothing to guess and it proceeds. The multiplication is the expensive one: it produces a wrong value in silence and the failure surfaces much later somewhere that looks unrelated, whereas the TypeError points at the exact line the instant it runs.

exam.prompt: Write `is_even_split(total, people)` giving `True` when the total divides among that many people with nothing left over, and `False` otherwise.
exam.solution:
def is_even_split(total, people):
    return total % people == 0
exam.explain: The leftover is exactly what `%` produces, and comparing it with zero turns that number into the True or False the question asked for. Comparing the two divisions instead - checking that `total / people` equals `total // people` - happens to pass these tests, but it does the work twice and leans on a float comparison that stops being reliable for large values.
